_instructions._readme: HOW TO ADD/UPDATE RESOURCES DATA — Read this before editing!
_howToAddExternalLink: 1. Add a new object to the 'externalLinks' array.
3. Fill in 'name', 'description', and 'url'. For a 'platform', you can add 'logo': put a square PNG/SVG in assets/resource-logos/ and set 'logo' to its path.
4. Upload resources.json to S3 and hard-refresh the site.
_howToAddCheatsheetEntry: 1. Add a new object to the 'cheatsheet' array.
2. Set 'service' to the AWS service name.
3. Set 'icon' to an emoji fallback (shown if image fails to load).
4. Set 'iconImg' to 'assets/service-icons/<filename>.png' if an icon file exists.

5. Set 'category' to one of: Compute, Storage, Database, Networking, Security, Integration, Analytics, Serverless, Management, Migration, Containers, Cost, Machine Learning, Media, Frontend, Developer Tools, Other.
6. Write a short one-liner 'description' of what the service does.
7. Add relevant 'keywords' as an array of strings.
8. Upload resources.json and the PNG to S3, then hard-refresh the site.

_fields.externalLinks[].name: Display name of the channel, person, repo, or platform.
_fields.externalLinks[].description: Short note on why it's useful for SAA prep.
_fields.externalLinks[].logo: OPTIONAL. Path to the platform's logo, e.g. 'assets/resource-logos/kodekloud.png' (square, about 64x64 px, PNG or SVG). Shown on the card; without it platforms show a screen icon. YouTube, GitHub and LinkedIn links don't need it: they show the brand's own logo.
_fields.cheatsheet[].icon: Emoji fallback shown if the image fails to load.
_fields.cheatsheet[].iconImg: Path to the PNG icon in assets/service-icons/. Omit if no icon available.
_fields.cheatsheet[].description: One-line description of what the service does.
_fields.cheatsheet[].keywords: Array of exam-relevant keywords and synonyms for search.
_fields.cheatsheet[].practiceTopic: OPTIONAL. The Practice topic for this service's 'Practice questions' button, when its name doesn't match a topic on its own.
_fields.comparisons[]: 'Commonly confused' sets shown in Resources. id, title, question (one line on why they get confused), columns (the services), rows [{label, values (one per column)}], pick (when to choose each), traps (exam traps), practiceTopics (Practice tab topic names), cheatsheet (cheat-sheet service names that link to this comparison).

comparisons.title: Security groups vs network ACLs
comparisons.question: Both filter traffic in a VPC. The exam asks which one can block a specific IP, and why return traffic fails.

rows.label: Applies to
values: An instance's network interface
A whole subnet

rows.label: State
values: Stateful: return traffic is allowed automatically
Stateless: return traffic needs its own rule (ephemeral ports 1024–65535)

rows.label: Rule types
values: Allow rules only
Allow and deny rules

rows.label: Evaluation
values: All rules are evaluated together
Rules are evaluated in number order; the first match wins

rows.label: Default
values: A new group denies all inbound and allows all outbound
The default NACL allows everything; a new custom NACL denies everything until you add rules

rows.label: Can reference
values: Other security groups (e.g. allow traffic from the ALB's group)
CIDR ranges only

pick: Security group: control which sources can reach specific instances, especially by referencing another tier's security group.
Network ACL: block a specific IP address or range at the subnet edge (security groups can't deny).
traps: "Block one malicious IP" → a NACL deny rule. Security groups have no deny rules.
Outbound responses failing through a custom NACL usually means the ephemeral port range isn't allowed.

comparisons.title: SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge vs Kinesis Data Streams
comparisons.question: All four move messages between components. The difference is who pulls, who gets a copy, and whether the data can be replayed.

rows.label: Model
values: Queue: consumers poll and each message is processed once
Pub/sub: pushes a copy to every subscriber
Event bus: rules route matching events to targets
Stream: ordered records that many consumers read independently

rows.label: Retention
values: Up to 14 days (default 4)
None: delivered or lost (use an SQS subscription to keep it)
None by default; optional archive and replay
24 hours by default, up to 365 days; consumers can re-read

rows.label: Ordering
values: FIFO queues: strict order, exactly-once processing
FIFO topics (with SQS FIFO subscribers)
No ordering guarantee
Ordered within a shard (by partition key)

rows.label: Typical sources
values: Your application
Your application, CloudWatch alarms, S3 events
AWS service events, SaaS partners, schedules, other accounts
High-volume producers: clickstreams, logs, IoT

rows.label: Scaling
values: Fully managed, nearly unlimited throughput (standard)
Fully managed
Fully managed
Provisioned shards, or on-demand mode

pick: SQS: decouple tiers and buffer spikes so a slow consumer never drops work.
SNS: fan one message out to many subscribers (email, SMS, Lambda, several SQS queues).
EventBridge: react to AWS or SaaS events with content-based rules, or run scheduled jobs.
Kinesis Data Streams: real-time analytics where several applications read the same ordered data, with replay.
traps: Fan-out to several queues that each process every message → SNS topic with SQS subscriptions.
"Multiple consumers must read the same records, in order, and replay them" → Kinesis, not SQS.
"Trigger on an EC2 state change or an AWS API call" → EventBridge rule.

comparisons.title: EBS vs EFS vs FSx vs S3
comparisons.question: Block, file and object storage. Most questions turn on how many clients need access, which OS they run, and from where.

rows.label: Storage type
values: Block volume
File system (NFS)
File system: Windows (SMB), Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS
Object storage (HTTP API)

rows.label: Who can attach
values: One EC2 instance in the same AZ (io1/io2 Multi-Attach within one AZ)
Thousands of Linux clients across AZs and on-premises
Windows or Linux clients, depending on the FSx type
Anything that can call the API, from anywhere

rows.label: Scope
values: One Availability Zone
Regional (multi-AZ), or One Zone
Single-AZ or Multi-AZ, depending on the type
Regional, 11 nines of durability

rows.label: Capacity
values: You provision the size
Grows and shrinks automatically
You provision capacity
Unlimited

rows.label: Typical use
values: Boot volumes, databases on EC2
Shared content and home directories for Linux
Windows file shares with Active Directory; HPC scratch on Lustre
Backups, data lakes, static websites, media

pick: EBS: low-latency disk for a single instance.
EFS: a shared POSIX file system for many Linux instances across AZs.
FSx for Windows File Server: SMB shares with Active Directory. FSx for Lustre: high-performance computing, linked to S3.
S3: durable, cheap storage accessed over HTTP, with lifecycle tiers down to Glacier.
traps: Windows + SMB + Active Directory → FSx for Windows File Server. EFS is NFS for Linux only.
"Shared file system across AZs" rules out EBS, which is tied to one AZ.
HPC that reads and writes S3 data at high throughput → FSx for Lustre.

comparisons.title: ALB vs NLB vs GWLB
comparisons.question: Three load balancers for three layers. The deciding words are usually HTTP routing, static IP, or third-party appliances.

rows.label: Layer
values: 7: HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC
4: TCP, UDP, TLS
3: IP packets (GENEVE on port 6081)

rows.label: Routing
values: By path, host, header, query string; Lambda can be a target
By port; millions of requests per second at very low latency
Sends traffic through a fleet of virtual appliances and back

rows.label: Static IP
values: No: a DNS name (put Global Accelerator in front for static IPs)
Yes: one static IP per AZ, Elastic IPs supported
Not applicable

rows.label: Typical use
values: Web apps, microservices, containers
Gaming, IoT, non-HTTP protocols, IP allow-listing
Third-party firewalls, IDS/IPS, deep packet inspection

pick: ALB: route HTTP requests by URL or host to different services.
NLB: extreme performance, TCP/UDP, or clients that need a fixed IP address.
GWLB: insert and scale third-party network appliances transparently.
traps: "Customers allow-list our IP addresses" → NLB (Elastic IPs) or Global Accelerator, not ALB.
"Route /api to one service and /images to another" → ALB path-based routing.

comparisons.title: CloudFront vs Global Accelerator
comparisons.question: Both use the AWS edge network to make a global app faster. Only one of them caches.

rows.label: What it does
values: CDN: caches content at edge locations close to users
Routes TCP/UDP traffic over the AWS backbone to the nearest healthy regional endpoint

rows.label: Caching
values: Yes
No

rows.label: Protocols
values: HTTP and HTTPS (including WebSocket)
TCP and UDP

rows.label: IP addresses
values: Changing edge IPs behind a DNS name
Two static anycast IP addresses

rows.label: Failover
values: Origin groups fail over between origins
Health checks shift traffic between Regions in under a minute

rows.label: Typical use
values: Websites, video, APIs, S3 static content
Gaming, VoIP, IoT, multi-Region apps needing static IPs

pick: CloudFront: cache static or dynamic web content near users and protect an S3 origin (OAC).
Global Accelerator: non-HTTP traffic, static IPs, or fast Regional failover without caching.
traps: UDP game traffic with global users → Global Accelerator. CloudFront doesn't carry UDP.
"Cache images close to users" → CloudFront. Global Accelerator never caches.

comparisons.title: RDS Multi-AZ vs read replicas
comparisons.question: One is for availability, the other for read scaling. Questions usually describe the goal, not the feature.

rows.label: Purpose
values: High availability: automatic failover
Scale reads; cross-Region replicas also help disaster recovery

rows.label: Replication
values: Synchronous
Asynchronous

rows.label: Serve reads?
values: Single standby: no. Multi-AZ DB cluster: two readable standbys
Yes, each replica has its own endpoint

rows.label: Failover
values: Automatic; the endpoint name stays the same
Manual: promote a replica to a standalone database

rows.label: Location
values: Another AZ in the same Region
Same AZ, another AZ, or another Region

pick: Multi-AZ: survive an AZ or instance failure with no application change.
Read replicas: offload reporting or read-heavy traffic from the primary.
traps: "Reporting queries slow down the production database" → read replica, not Multi-AZ.
"Automatic failover with no change to the connection string" → Multi-AZ.

comparisons.title: Site-to-Site VPN vs Direct Connect
comparisons.question: Two ways to connect a data center to AWS. Time to set up, consistency and encryption decide it.

rows.label: Path
values: Encrypted IPsec tunnels over the public internet
A private, dedicated connection through a Direct Connect location

rows.label: Setup time
values: Minutes to hours
Weeks to months

rows.label: Bandwidth
values: Up to 1.25 Gbps per tunnel
Dedicated 1, 10 or 100 Gbps; hosted 50 Mbps to 10 Gbps

rows.label: Encryption
values: Built in (IPsec)
Not encrypted by default: add MACsec or run a VPN over it

rows.label: Latency
values: Varies with the internet
Consistent

pick: VPN: a quick, low-cost hybrid link, or a backup path for Direct Connect.
Direct Connect: large, steady transfers with consistent performance.
traps: "Encrypt traffic over Direct Connect" → a VPN over the DX connection (or MACsec).
"Need connectivity this week" → VPN. Direct Connect takes weeks to provision.

comparisons.title: Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store
comparisons.question: Both store secrets encrypted with KMS. Rotation and cost separate them.

rows.label: Automatic rotation
values: Built in (RDS, Aurora, Redshift, DocumentDB; Lambda for others)
No native rotation

rows.label: Cost
values: Per secret per month, plus API calls
Standard parameters free; advanced parameters paid

rows.label: Size limit
values: 64 KB per secret
4 KB standard, 8 KB advanced

rows.label: Cross-Region replication
values: Yes
No

rows.label: Typical use
values: Database credentials that must rotate
Configuration values, feature flags, non-rotating secrets (SecureString)

pick: Secrets Manager: credentials that must rotate automatically.
Parameter Store: configuration and simple secrets at the lowest cost.
traps: "Rotate the database password automatically every 30 days" → Secrets Manager.
"Store configuration values cheaply" → Parameter Store standard tier.
